pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 12–14 — interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ (1 ≤ A < 10, n an integer); convert between ordinary numbers and standard form.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ, 1 ≤ A < 10, where n is a positive or negative integer.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 8.EE.A.3 (express and estimate very large/small quantities as a single digit times a power of ten) and 8.EE.A.4 (operate with and compare numbers in scientific notation).
• Operational details: Standard form re-expresses a number as one digit before the point (1 ≤ A < 10) times a power of ten; positive n for large numbers, negative n for small. Converting is the ×10/÷10 place-value shift counted: n is how many places the point moves. Compare by exponent first (bigger power = bigger number, for positive values), then by A. Enforce the 1 ≤ A < 10 normalisation (34 × 10⁶ is not standard form).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 12): 'Write 4,500,000 in standard form.' Tier B: 'Convert 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to an ordinary number.' Tier C: 'Order 6.1×10⁵, 9.8×10⁴ and 2.3×10⁶ and explain your method.'
bestPractices: Connect standard form directly to the ×10/÷10 place-value shift — the exponent counts how many places the digits move
Enforce the normalisation 1 ≤ A < 10 and use non-examples (34×10⁶, 0.5×10³) to police it
Handle positive n (large numbers) and negative n (small numbers) together so the exponent's sign carries meaning
Compare numbers in standard form by exponent first, then mantissa A, rather than converting everything back
Ground very large/small quantities in real contexts (astronomical distances, atomic sizes) so standard form is seen as a tool for scale
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with the point shifting n places for ×10ⁿ
A × 10ⁿ template with a normalisation guard on A (1 ≤ A < 10)
Number line / scale strip spanning many orders of magnitude
Ordering cards comparing by exponent then mantissa
commonMisconceptions: Miscounting the exponent — using the number of zeros incorrectly, or wrong sign for small numbers
Moving the digits the wrong direction for negative exponents (3.2×10⁻⁴ written as 32000)
Comparing by mantissa first and ignoring the exponent's dominance
Thinking a negative exponent makes the number negative rather than small/positive

learn.summary: For learners aged 12–14: interpret, convert and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is any integer. The central idea is that the exponent counts and directs the ×10/÷10 place-value shift — positive n for large numbers, negative n for small positive numbers — and that A must be kept in the range 1 ≤ A < 10 so each number has a unique form. For positive values, comparison is done by exponent first, then by A to break ties.

activities.title: Dial-the-exponent place-value converter
feedback: If you converted 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to 32000, you moved the wrong way — a negative exponent means ÷10 each time, so the decimal point moves LEFT (the digits shift right into smaller place values), giving 0.00032. Convert back: 0.00032 = 3.2 ÷ 10,000 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴.

If you left A outside 1 ≤ A < 10 (e.g. 34 × 10⁵ or 0.34 × 10⁷), adjust A and n together: making A ten times smaller means n increases by one, so 34 × 10⁵ = 3.4 × 10⁶; making A ten times larger means n decreases by one, so 0.34 × 10⁷ = 3.4 × 10⁶ — the ordinary number must stay the same.
If your exponent is off by one, convert back and count: 4.7 × 10³ = 4,700, which is not 47,000, so recount the place-shifts to get 4.7 × 10⁴.
activities.rationale: Linking a mantissa–exponent control to a live place-value chart makes conversion and the 1 ≤ A < 10 normalisation visible as place-value movement, directly addressing the common errors of wrong-direction shifts for negative exponents and mis-normalised A. A live converter with a normalisation guard and a scale strip are optional mechanisms that make this concrete; the same learning can be done on paper with a place-value chart and counted point-moves. The interactive mechanism is a proposed, untested scaffold.
learnerActions: Set up two linked views: an ordinary number shown on a place-value chart, and an A × 10ⁿ expression you can change.

Starting with A = 4.5 and n = 0, increase n and watch the digits slide LEFT into higher place-value columns (equivalently, the decimal point moves right) one column per unit of n until 4.5 becomes 4,500,000 (4.5 × 10⁶); describe what each change of n does to the place value.

Now set A = 3.2 and n = −4; watch the digits slide RIGHT four columns into smaller place values (equivalently, the decimal point moves left four places) to give 0.00032, and state in words why the result is small but still positive.

Deliberately type an expression like 34 × 10⁵ and notice it is flagged as not in standard form; renormalise it yourself to 3.4 × 10⁶ by adjusting A and n together, then check the ordinary number is unchanged.
Record a short rule: 'n is how many places the point moves — right for positive n, left for negative n — and n never makes the number negative.'
activities.intendedInsight: Standard form is the ×10/÷10 place-value shift turned into notation: the exponent counts and directs how many columns the digits move, and a negative exponent makes a number small, not negative.

activities.title: Order standard-form numbers by scale
feedback: If you said 9.8 × 10⁴ > 3.2 × 10⁵ because 9.8 > 3.2, convert both: 98,000 vs 320,000 — the larger exponent wins, so compare exponents first and use A only to break ties.

If you ranked by coefficient alone — for example calling 9 × 10² the largest because its coefficient 9 is the biggest — remember 9 × 10² = 900 but 1.5 × 10³ = 1,500: a higher power of ten outweighs a larger coefficient.
Good: comparing exponents first and converting back as a check are two reliable ways to confirm your order.
activities.rationale: Ordering tasks that force a conflict between a large mantissa and a larger exponent target the documented 'compare by mantissa first' error and establish the exponent-first comparison rule for positive, normalised values.
learnerActions: Place 6.1 × 10⁵, 9.8 × 10⁴ and 2.3 × 10⁶ in order from smallest to largest; a magnitude scale strip can help you position them.
First decide the order by comparing exponents only (for these positive numbers, a bigger power means a bigger number), then use A only to break ties.
Test the trap directly: decide which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴; justify by exponent (5 beats 4) and confirm by converting to 320,000 vs 98,000.
Order 2 × 10³, 9 × 10² and 1.5 × 10³ and explain why 9 × 10² is smallest even though its coefficient 9 is the largest.
Write one sentence explaining your comparison method.
activities.intendedInsight: For positive numbers in standard form with A normalised to 1 ≤ A < 10, the exponent dominates the comparison; the mantissa A only matters when exponents are equal.

activities.title: Consolidate with two-way conversion checks
feedback: 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032, not 32000 — a negative exponent moves the decimal point left (the digits shift right into smaller place values).
47,000 = 4.7 × 10⁴ and 0.0032 = 3.2 × 10⁻³; if you got 4.7 × 10³ or 3.2 × 10⁻², recount by converting back.

If an answer fails its reverse-check, the error is often an off-by-one in the exponent, but it may be a wrong-direction shift (such as 32000 for 3.2 × 10⁻⁴) — recount the point moves and check their direction.
activities.rationale: Converting both directions and comparing standard-form numbers are cleanly checkable tasks that consolidate the procedure once the place-value shift is understood; the reverse-check builds self-correction. This reinforces fluency rather than first-time concept building. The reverse-check routine is a proposed practice, not an empirically validated intervention.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: 4,500,000 = ___ × 10ⁿ, keeping 1 ≤ A < 10 and stating n.
Convert 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ to an ordinary number, resisting the tempting wrong answer of 32000.
Convert 47,000 and 0.0032 into standard form, then convert each answer back to check you land on the original number.
For every answer, verify by reversing the conversion so an off-by-one exponent is caught immediately.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion, with a reverse-check habit, catches exponent miscounts and wrong-direction shifts.

activities.title: Argue about the negative exponent
feedback: If you said 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ is negative, note that 10⁻⁴ = 1/10,000, a positive fraction, so 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032 > 0.
A convincing argument separates 'sign of the number' from 'sign of the exponent': the exponent only tells you how many times to multiply or divide by 10.
activities.rationale: A structured dialogue can surface and challenge the 'negative exponent = negative number' misconception by demanding justification; it may complement, rather than replace, the procedural digit-shift practice. Note that a dialogue can prompt justification but does not by itself exercise the procedural conversion.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Is 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ a negative number? Convince me.'
Explain, using 10⁻³ = 1/10³, why a negative exponent produces a small positive amount, not a negative value.
Contrast 10³, 10⁰ and 10⁻³ on a place-value scale to show how the exponent's sign controls size but never the sign of the number.
activities.intendedInsight: The sign of the exponent controls how large or small the number is, separately from whether the number itself is positive or negative.

activities.title: Ground standard form in real scales
feedback: Check that, in a base unit such as metres, very small quantities (atomic sizes) use negative exponents and very large ones (astronomical distances) use positive exponents.
A static scale illustrates purpose well but cannot perform or check your conversions — do the conversions yourself and verify them.
activities.rationale: Grounding very large and very small quantities in real contexts motivates standard form as a tool for scale. An annotated scale is illustrative; it supports motivation and reading of values but does not by itself enforce normalisation or exercise conversion.
learnerActions: Examine an orders-of-magnitude scale (for example from a grain of sand to a galaxy, or atomic size to astronomical distance) and express several labelled quantities in standard form.
For each quantity, state whether n is positive or negative and what that tells you about the size.
Explain why standard form is useful for writing very large and very small quantities compactly.
activities.intendedInsight: Standard form is a practical tool for expressing and comparing quantities that span many orders of magnitude.

constraints: Enforce 1 ≤ A < 10; use non-examples such as 34 × 10⁶ and 0.5 × 10³ to make the normalisation rule explicit.
Teach positive n (large numbers) and negative n (small positive numbers) together so the sign of the exponent carries meaning.
A fixed scale poster or illustration motivates and displays values but cannot perform conversions or enforce normalisation; use it alongside, not instead of, active conversion practice.

Recognition-only or single-answer selection consolidates fluency but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify conversions; include tasks where learners produce the conversion and check it.
Keep the sign of the number distinct from the sign of the exponent throughout: a negative exponent never makes a number negative.
Scope the exponent-first comparison rule to positive, normalised values (1 ≤ A < 10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources are national/standards documents (listed as verified:false in the source row); they support the curriculum scope (interpret/convert/compare standard form; express and estimate very large/small quantities using powers of ten) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity, mechanism or medium. Accordingly, every activity's sourceClaims is [], because each rationale rests on a specific teaching mechanism or framing (interactive converter, conflict-ordering, reverse-check habit, real-scale motivation) that no source addresses.

The original row's claim that '3D adds nothing' for this symbolic topic was removed as unsupported catalog-ranking boilerplate; standard form is symbolic and essentially one-dimensional, so a spatial 3D model is simply not the natural representation here, but no universal necessity or medium-superiority claim is asserted.

Self-audit of worked values: 4.5 × 10⁶ = 4,500,000; 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00032; 47,000 = 4.7 × 10⁴; 0.0032 = 3.2 × 10⁻³; 34 × 10⁵ = 3.4 × 10⁶; 6.1 × 10⁻³ = 0.0061; 3.2 × 10⁵ = 320,000 > 9.8 × 10⁴ = 98,000; 2 × 10³ = 2,000, 9 × 10² = 900, 1.5 × 10³ = 1,500 — all consistent and retained. The deliberately wrong distractor 32000 for 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ is only ever presented as an error to be corrected, never as a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Is 10⁻³ a negative number or a small positive one? How do you know?
Convert your 4.7 × 10⁴ back to an ordinary number — do you land on 47,000?

errorPatterns.nextMove: State the rule and its purpose (one non-zero digit before the point, so every number has a unique form). Adjust A and the exponent together on a few examples.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The coefficient is not a single non-zero digit before the point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a negative exponent as making the number negative: reads 6.1 × 10⁻³ as −6100 or −0.0061
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate sign of number from sign of exponent: 10⁻³ = 1/10³, a small POSITIVE amount. Contrast 10³, 10⁰, 10⁻³ on a place-value scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by the mantissa, ignoring the power: says 9.8 × 10⁴ > 3.2 × 10⁵ because 9.8 > 3.2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert both to ordinary form (320,000 vs 98,000) to expose the size gap; then formalise: compare exponents first, mantissa only to break ties.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The larger number is chosen by the coefficient alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place-shifts, giving an off-by-one exponent (47,000 → 4.7 × 10³, or 0.0032 → 3.2 × 10⁻²)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — have them convert back to check (4.7 × 10³ = 4,700 ≠ 47,000) and recount the decimal-point moves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A is correct but n is one out.

responseLevels.gap: Writes A outside 1 ≤ A < 10 or treats a negative index as a negative number.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions for large and small numbers keeping 1 ≤ A < 10, handles negative indices as small positives, and compares/orders by exponent then mantissa.
responseLevels.partial: Converts straightforward large numbers but errs on small numbers, negative indices, or comparison.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Write 47,000 in standard form. Write 0.0032 in standard form. Write 6.1 × 10⁻³ as an ordinary number. Then: which is larger, 3.2 × 10⁵ or 9.8 × 10⁴?' Watch the value of A they choose, how they treat the negative index, and how they compare.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each item targets one documented slip: the two conversions check whether A is kept in 1 ≤ A < 10 and whether the exponent is counted correctly in each direction; 6.1 × 10⁻³ checks the 'negative index = negative number' error; the comparison checks whether they order by exponent or wrongly by the mantissa.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10 and n a positive or negative integer.
